newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD - Australian markets focus on RBA report.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-WEEK AHEAD - Australian markets focus on RBA report.

text.p: Australian financial markets face a fairly scarce calendar this week, with the major event having already been largely pre-empted by Reserve Bank of Australia governor Ian Macfarlane comments last week.

Equity markets, however, are in the middle of the half-year profit reporting period -- with mixed to disappointing results for many companies. (See timetable of company profits at end of this report.)

Traders and investors will place a special focus this week on the fortunes of biscuit maker Arnotts Ltd which has been forced to remove its product from shelves in New South Wales and Queensland due to an extortion threat. Its shares slumped last Friday when brokers had the first chance to trade the stock in response to the threat and a slump in first half profits.

The release of the RBA's quarterly assessment of the economy is always an eagerly awaited event, but in the climate of uncertainty surrounding rates, the RBA's comments will be of great importance. The RBA report will be released on Tuesday.

Adding to the expectation is that the RBA has pushed back by one month the release of its quarterly report, meaning it is four months since the last report, and the first major statement on RBA thinking since the December 11 rate cut.
However, markets got a taste of the RBA's thinking last Tuesday when Macfarlane said the answer to the question posed after he delivered a speech was basically what would be in the quarterly article.

Macfarlane said there were signs that the effects of the three rate cuts were starting to come through, and that the economy was looking stronger in 1997 than 1996. He pointed to strength in housing, investment and some signs of employment growth.

Combined with last Thursday's stronger than expected labour force data and some of the major banks delivering consumers a de-facto easing by cutting mortgage rates, economists have wound back their expectations of another easing.
Two weeks ago economists saw an even money chance of a fourth rate cut. On Friday, the median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters had dropped to 30 percent.

"Take a cautious RBA Governor, add a dash of solid economic activity data, and we have a reliable formula for producing interest rates on hold," Citibank Australia senior economist Annette Beacher said.
On the data front, the two main releases are January imports on Wednesday and December quarter company profits on Thursday.
The imports release will be the last in the current format, following the demise last month of the monthly current account deficit.
Imports are expected to have risen for the sixth consecutive month in January, with economists looking for strength in capital imports.

Company profits are seen flat in the quarter, following on from a small rise in the September quarter, and reflecting the soft economic conditions in the second half of the year. Those on the soft side of expectations point to the weak retail conditions, but others said the retail weakness was not universal across the economy.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash yield 7.31 pct, 3-yr 6.71)

Australian bonds will start the week on a stronger note, encouraged by the U.S. Treasuries market which finished higher last Friday in response to a favourable wholesale inflation report. However, trading is likely to be fairly slow over the next couple of dayS as the U.S. is closed today for Presidents Day.

Reduced expectations of a monetary policy easing could keep a fragile tone at the short end, although the extent that this part of the curve has weakened in the past week or so could see the market now react more to any weak data.

"Given the market's perception that interest rates are on hold in the medium term, stronger than expected data in the coming months are unlikely to see the market sell-off significantly at the short-end," said Su-Lin Ong, fixed income economist at Hambros Australia.
"However, any indicators suggesting weak growth or very well behaved wages are likely to see the market rally more strongly," she added.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri US$0.7641, New York US$0.7653)

The Australian dollar is likely to trade in a tight range this week, with little domestic data to influence the currency and local traders to take a wait-and-see attitude while the yen struggles to hold ground against the U.S. dollar.
The local dollar ended at US$0.7641 on Friday and gained some ground overnight in New York, where the U.S. dollar hit a four-year high against the yen.
U.S. markets will be closed on Monday for Presidents Day, another reason for steady trade in the Australian dollar at least early in the week.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri All Ords 2,482.60 -13.80)
The Australian share market is likely to consolidate this week after passing the 2,500 barrier for the first time last week.
Investors slapped the market back last Friday in a sign that further gains are likely to be hard-won.
Traders said any dive on Wall Street would not improve the mood. The U.S. market took a small step back on Friday.
"U.S. strength helps but it is not essential. Any fall will not likely be taken to heart unless it is a dramatic drop," a Brisbane broker said.
All eyes are on individual companies this week as the results season continues. Thursday is choc-a-block with numbers but Friday has little scheduled at this stage.
